header.incumbent: Homegrown billing system built by a former employee who has left
header.tag_why: Nobody switched: the CFO froze all new vendor projects after a Q3 miss, but the deal was already exposed because finance saw it as a 'nice to have' and Owen never got the customer-specific payback number he said he needed to get it past Diane.

messaging_changes.current_line: Billing that helps you grow revenue.
messaging_changes.change: For product and engineering buyers replacing a homegrown billing system: 'Stop billing being a tax on the roadmap. Change a price, add a trial or prorate in a few clicks, instead of spending a quarter of engineering time on every pricing change.'
messaging_changes.why: The champion rejected the revenue-growth framing outright ('we're not trying to grow revenue with billing, we're trying to stop it being a tax on the roadmap.') and described the demo himself as 'a quarter of roadmap in five minutes'.

messaging_changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
messaging_changes.change: Use the study only as a door-opener. When a buyer asks about payback, reply: 'Let's build your own payback number together: what your current billing costs you today, and what changes when you switch.' Offer a dated working session within days instead of sending the general ROI deck.
messaging_changes.why: The rep sent the general ROI deck with the study, the champion said 'I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours', and the session to build that number never happened before Q3 closed.

messaging_changes.change: Add a finance-facing companion piece the champion can forward to the CFO when replacing homegrown billing. It should answer 'is this on fire?' with the monthly cost of keeping the current system: engineering time per pricing change, billing errors, and subscriptions that lapse 'because the card fails and nobody chases it' (tie the last item to M10 smart retries). The goal is to show the cost of doing nothing, not to list features.
messaging_changes.why: Finance treated the project as a 'nice to have' under an 'if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded' rule, and the customer named the cost inputs (including lapsed subscriptions from failed cards), but 'We never added it up.'

messaging_changes.change: For buyers moving off a homegrown billing system, add a migration proof point: an offer to talk to a reference customer who has made the same move, not only a migration doc.
messaging_changes.why: The rep says 'We had a doc for that. He wanted to talk to someone who'd done it.', so a written migration claim was not enough proof for this buyer.

evidence.excerpt: There wasn't one big thing.
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: Renee

evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Not really. He wanted it done before they launched a new pricing tier, but the tier didn't have a date either.
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: Renee

trigger.insight: This was a long-held wish of one VP, not an event. There was no deadline, and the pricing tier it was tied to had no date either. The pain was real but chronic, which is exactly the kind of problem Diane's 'if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded' rule screens out. The deal never had a compelling event, and nobody built one.
trigger.messaging: When there is no trigger, the opener has to create urgency by putting a cost on time: what each quarter-long pricing change and each delayed tier costs the business, instead of an aspirational 'grow globally' line (M1).

decider.insight: The person who held the money was never in a meeting, and everything we know about her comes through Owen. Paper went out while the economic buyer had only ever seen us through a generic ROI deck that Owen himself said wouldn't get past her. The plan to bring her in 'at the end' handed the business case to a champion who had told us he couldn't make it alone.
decider.messaging: Our material for product and engineering buyers needs a finance-facing companion piece the champion can forward to the CFO, framed around cost of the status quo rather than features.

evidence.label: quote

competitor.insight: The real competitor was the status quo, and it won by default. The rep's 'as far as I know' leaves open whether other vendors were looked at. The only change in the customer's questions was the late turn toward finance and payback. That turn was the moment the decision moved from Owen's desk to Diane's, and we answered it as a content request rather than a deal risk.
competitor.messaging: Against 'do nothing', position on what doing nothing costs (engineering time, billing errors, lapsed subscriptions) rather than on our advantages over other vendors.

evidence.label: quote
evidence.speaker: Owen

message.insight: The demo landed, and Owen translated it himself into roadmap time saved. Our billing message (M7, 'grow revenue') was explicitly rejected, which is more than silence. The rep first said nothing got silence, so this rejection nearly went unreported. Our value story never reached finance at all, so we can't say how it would have landed there.
message.messaging: For replacing homegrown billing, swap 'Billing that helps you grow revenue' (M7) for roadmap-recovery language, for example pricing changes in minutes instead of a quarter of engineering time.

evidence.excerpt: We were going to set up a session to build one. Then Q3 closed.
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: Renee

decided.insight: The freeze ended it, but the deal was lost before that. Owen asked for payback about a month before the freeze and got the generic study (M6). He said outright it wouldn't work, and the session to build their own number had not happened when Q3 closed. The rep calls it 'timing' and says nothing could have been done, which hides an unanswered buyer request. A deal with its own business case might still have been frozen, but it would have gone into the freeze ranked as something other than a 'nice to have'.
decided.messaging: Treat 'Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study' (M6) as a door-opener only, and make the customer-specific payback model the standard next step whenever a buyer asks about payback.

gaps.insight: The customer handed us the inputs for their business case: engineering time, billing errors and lapsed landlord subscriptions from failed cards. The lapsed subscriptions are a recovery problem that M10 speaks to directly, yet nobody added it up. On migration, Owen asked about moving subscriptions without re-collecting cards and about a staged move, and he wanted a peer who had done it, not a doc. The transcript doesn't say whether a reference was ever offered.
gaps.messaging: Build a cost-of-homegrown-billing worksheet (engineering time per pricing change, billing errors, revenue lost to unchased failed cards), and back the migration claim with reference customers who moved existing subscriptions without re-collecting cards.

evidence.excerpt: we're not trying to grow revenue with billing, we're trying to stop it being a tax on the roadmap.
evidence.label: quote
evidence.speaker: Owen

evidence.excerpt: I can't get this past Diane without a number that's ours.
evidence.label: quote
evidence.speaker: Owen

evidence.excerpt: if it isn't on fire, it isn't funded.
evidence.label: quote
evidence.speaker: Diane (via Owen)

evidence.excerpt: Owen said finance saw it as a nice to have.
evidence.label: fact
evidence.speaker: Owen

language.insight: Two vocabularies: product talks about a 'tax on the roadmap', while finance talks about whether something is 'on fire' and calls this a 'nice to have'. Our messaging spoke neither one; it talked about revenue growth and a third-party study. The phrase 'a number that's ours' is the clearest statement of what finance-side proof has to look like.
language.messaging: Adopt 'a tax on the roadmap' as the product-buyer framing for billing replacement, and give champions a way to show finance the fire: their own monthly cost of keeping the homegrown system.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen: did Diane ever see our proposal or the ROI deck, and was Pikeview ranked or cut specifically, or frozen along with every other vendor project?

gaps.question: Did Owen evaluate any other vendor or a rebuild of the homegrown system?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen directly whether any other vendor, or an internal rebuild, was considered.

gaps.question: Was the migration reference (someone who'd done it) ever provided?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee whether a reference customer was offered or scheduled, and if not, why not.

gaps.question: Why wasn't the session to build their payback number held during the month between the ask and the freeze?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Renee what happened in that month: was the session ever proposed with a date, and who was blocking it?

gaps.question: When is renewal season, and when does the freeze lift?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen when the vendor freeze is expected to lift and when renewal season falls, to judge whether 'next year' is realistic.

gaps.question: What does the homegrown system actually cost them?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Owen for estimates of engineering time per pricing change, billing error volume, and lapsed subscriptions from failed cards, so we can build their number before the freeze lifts.

close.rep_takeaway: When a champion starts asking for things 'for finance', the real decider has entered the deal. Treat it as the most urgent ask in the cycle: build the customer's own number with them within days, and use that work as the reason to get the CFO into a meeting. A generic study the champion has already said won't work isn't a response, and 'it's timing' shouldn't be the conclusion when a buyer's request was still open.
